query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Moderate thermal aging of as‐cast MgAlCuZnGd high-entropy alloys induces controlled diffusion of metastable Mg that leads to the nucleation of Mg‐rich intermetallic precipitates and the in situ formation of a continuous MgO/complex spinel oxide network at grain boundaries, which then retards high-temperature oxidation and improves corrosion resistance compared to the unaged alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast non‐equilibrium MgAlCuZnGd high‐entropy alloy with density below 6 g/cm³
generation.intervention: Thermal aging at 400 °C for 2 hours in air
generation.conditions: After aging, subject both aged and as‐cast samples to high-temperature oxidation tests (600–700 °C) and room-temperature corrosion tests using standard media
generation.structural_mediator: Nucleation and growth of Mg‐rich intermetallic precipitates and subsequent formation of a continuous MgO/complex spinel oxide network at the grain boundaries
generation.mechanism: Thermal aging activates diffusion of metastable Mg, which segregates and precipitates as Mg‐rich intermetallic phases. This transformation concurrently facilitates the formation of a protective oxide/spinel barrier that limits further oxidation and modifies the electrochemical pathways that govern corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Aged samples will display a thinner, more uniform, and adherent oxide scale with reduced oxidation kinetics at 600–700 °C, as well as improved passivation and lower corrosion current densities in standard corrosion tests compared to the as‐cast baseline.
generation.boundary: Lightweight HEA composition with density <6 g/cm³; aging conducted at a moderate temperature (400 °C for 2 h) in air; subsequent oxidation and corrosion tests performed under defined temperature (600–700 °C for oxidation) and standard conditions (room-temperature corrosion testing); aging parameters carefully chosen to retain non‐equilibrium characteristics.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal aging conditions (temperature/time) may vary, and excessive aging could overdrive the transformation to full equilibrium, potentially altering the predicted protective barrier formation. The precise quantitative improvement in corrosion and oxidation behavior is not precisely predictable without further experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of MgAlCuZnGd alloy samples: one group as-cast (baseline) and one group thermally aged at 400 °C for 2 hours in air. Subject both groups to high-temperature oxidation tests at 600–700 °C and standard room-temperature corrosion tests. Use microscopy and spectroscopy techniques to characterize oxide scale uniformity, thickness, and adherence. Perform electrochemical measurements to quantify corrosion passivation behavior.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and growth rate
Uniformity and adherence of the oxide layer (via SEM/EDS analysis)
Corrosion current densities and passivation current levels (via potentiodynamic polarization tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally aged samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxide growth rate, improved oxide uniformity/adherence, and lower corrosion current densities compared to the as-cast baseline, then the hypothesis that the transformation via thermal aging enhances protective barrier formation is falsified.

proposals.material_system: MgAlCuZnGd high‐entropy alloy (density <6 g/cm³) in as‐cast non-equilibrium state
proposals.intervention: Thermal aging at moderate temperatures (e.g., 400 °C for 2 hours) in air vs. unaged baseline
proposals.conditions: Expose both aged and as‐cast samples to elevated temperature oxidation (e.g., 600–700 °C) and standard corrosion media at room temperature
proposals.structural_mediator: Nucleation and growth of Mg‐rich intermetallic precipitates and subsequent in situ formation of protective MgO/complex spinel phases at grain boundaries
proposals.mechanism: Metastable Mg in the non‐equilibrium alloy diffuses and segregates upon moderate thermal activation, enabling the formation of continuous Mg‐oxide or composite intermetallic barriers that retard further oxidation and modify electrochemical corrosion pathways
proposals.predicted_outcome: Aged samples will show a more uniform and adherent oxide scale with lower oxide growth rates at high temperatures and improved passivation in corrosion tests compared to the baseline; lack of oxide phase development would falsify the hypothesis
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This direction tests the hypothesis that transformation from a metastable solid solution to a well‐defined intermetallic/oxide network mediates the functional properties of corrosion and high‐temperature oxidation, providing a controlled comparison (aged vs. as‐cast) under prescribed thermal boundary conditions

proposals.material_system: Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd high‐entropy alloy (non-equilibrium state; density <6 g/cm³)
proposals.intervention: Localized high-temperature oxidation experiments along regions of different Mg concentrations
proposals.conditions: Expose the graded alloy to high-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., 650 °C in an oxygen atmosphere) and ambient corrosion testing, comparing Mg-rich vs. Mg-lean regions
proposals.structural_mediator: Spatially dependent formation of intermetallic compounds, where higher Mg content areas more readily form Mg-rich oxides and/or intermetallic phases
proposals.mechanism: Intrinsic constituent-property differences drive region-specific phase evolution; in Mg-rich zones, faster diffusion and reactive oxidation yield a distinct, protective oxide/intermetallic microstructure that alters the local corrosion/oxidation kinetics relative to Mg-lean regions
proposals.predicted_outcome: Regions with higher Mg content will display thicker, more adherent and rapidly forming protective oxide scales and altered (e.g., lower) corrosion current densities compared to Mg-lean areas; a uniform oxidation/corrosion response regardless of composition would falsify this hypothesis
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: The study uses a controlled spatial comparison within a single sample to test the mechanistic hypothesis that local Mg-driven intermetallic and oxide evolutions govern corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior

proposals.material_system: AlMgₓTiSnZn lightweight high‐entropy alloy (density <6 g/cm³) in a non-equilibrium cast state
proposals.intervention: Application of a controlled cold rolling deformation to induce residual strain versus a non-deformed baseline
proposals.conditions: Perform deformation at room temperature to impose a uniform strain field, then subject both deformed and as-cast samples to accelerated corrosion (e.g., salt spray test) and high-temperature oxidation (e.g., 650 °C in dry air)
proposals.structural_mediator: Enhanced dislocation density and strain-induced nuclei that promote faster and more homogeneous segregation of Mg and formation of fine-scale intermetallic/oxide particles
proposals.mechanism: Mechanical deformation accelerates diffusion pathways and triggers non-equilibrium transformations; the induced defect network facilitates the formation of a refined intermetallic phase and oxide scale that improves passivation and oxidation resistance
proposals.predicted_outcome: The cold-rolled samples are predicted to exhibit a refined, homogeneous network of protective intermetallic/oxide phases leading to decreased corrosion rates and enhanced oxidation resistance relative to the unrolled state; if no significant structural or performance difference is observed, the hypothesis is falsified
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach tests whether mechanically activated transformation pathways in a non-equilibrium Mg-containing HEA alter the evolution of intermetallic phases and surface oxides, thus directly linking microstructural evolution to functional property changes

proposals.material_system: Mg-containing lightweight high‐entropy alloy (e.g., Al–Mg-rich system with density <6 g/cm³) obtained via induction melting
proposals.intervention: Surface modification via controlled in situ nano-scale MgO seeding (e.g., via a brief reactive sputtering or laser surface alloying) versus an unmodified surface
proposals.conditions: After surface modification, expose both seeded and unseeded samples to high-temperature oxidation (e.g., 700 °C in air) and corrosive aqueous environments
proposals.structural_mediator: Pre-formed nano MgO dispersions at the surface act as nucleation sites for preferential growth of a dense and protective oxide scale, and promote localized intermetallic stabilization beneath the surface
proposals.mechanism: The seeded MgO particles catalyze the subsequent oxidation and phase evolution process by reducing the activation barrier for oxide scale formation, leading to an altered, protective oxide microstructure that retards further degradation
proposals.predicted_outcome: Seeded samples are expected to develop a more uniform and adherent oxide layer with lower rates of high-temperature oxidation and improved corrosion resistance relative to the baseline unseeded alloy; a result where the surface modification does not alter or worsens performance would falsify the hypothesis
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This candidate directly tests the effect of an engineered surface oxide on subsequent non-equilibrium phase evolution and correlates the observed changes in high-temperature oxidation and corrosion behavior with the underlying transformation mechanism

critiques.addresses_problem: The approach directly probes how non‐equilibrium processing (via cold rolling) can accelerate transformation pathways in a Mg‐containing lightweight high‐entropy alloy. It links induced defects to microstructural evolution that governs corrosion and oxidation, thereby addressing the root cause.
critiques.constraints: The proposed material system (AlMgₓTiSnZn alloy with density <6 g/cm³) and room‐temperature deformation, followed by accelerated corrosion and oxidation tests, respect the specified constraints.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically plausible; cold rolling increases dislocation density, which can indeed enhance diffusion pathways and nucleate phase formation. However, the assumption that this leads to a uniformly beneficial refined intermetallic/oxide network in a non‐equilibrium HEA requires careful validation.
critiques.feasibility: Cold rolling and subsequent standard corrosion/oxidation testing methods (salt spray, high‐temp oxidation) are well established and feasible.
critiques.evidence: The approach builds upon prior observations in similar alloy systems (e.g., in Al–Mg‐rich and AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys) that link Mg content to phase stability, though an explicit record is not cited.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that the induced deformation may lead to heterogeneous strain recovery or unwanted segregation during subsequent high-temperature exposure, potentially obscuring the targeted mechanistic insight.
critiques.fix: Include an intermediate characterization step (e.g., microstructural and diffusion analysis at various stages prior to oxidation/corrosion tests) to ensure that the defect network is maintained and correlates with the expected phase evolution.

critiques.addresses_problem: This direction aims to modify the surface to seed MgO, potentially altering subsequent oxidation and corrosion behavior. However, it shifts the focus from intrinsic non‐equilibrium bulk transformation to an engineered surface intervention.
critiques.constraints: The design respects the density and material system constraints, though it employs an induction‐melted Al–Mg–rich alloy rather than a fully cast non-equilibrium alloy.
critiques.physical_soundness: The idea that pre-formed nano MgO seeds can catalyze oxide scale formation is physically sound, yet it may not capture the evolution from a metastable state as dictated by bulk transformations.
critiques.feasibility: Techniques like reactive sputtering or laser surface alloying are established, making the approach technically feasible.
critiques.evidence: The literature hints at surface passivation effects and engineered oxides in similar systems, but no specific prior record confirms that nano-seeding is effective in triggering the controlled non-equilibrium phase evolution in Mg-containing HEAs.
critiques.main_risk: The primary risk is that the externally introduced seed layer might dominate the oxidation process and mask the intrinsic evolution of the non-equilibrium microstructure, thus not directly testing the hypothesized mechanism.
critiques.fix: Modify the approach to include detailed bulk microstructural characterization beneath the seeded surface to ensure it reflects the intrinsic metastable transformation rather than solely a surface-engineered effect.

critiques.addresses_problem: The proposed experiment directly tests how local Mg concentration differences within a graded alloy affect phase evolution and, consequently, corrosion and oxidation behavior, which aligns well with the question’s focus.
critiques.constraints: It respects the design constraints (density <6 g/cm³) and uses a compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloy in its non‐equilibrium state.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism whereby intrinsic constituent-property differences drive localized phase transformations (with Mg-rich areas forming specific oxides/intermetallics) is physically sound.
critiques.feasibility: Localized high-temperature oxidation and corrosion testing are established methods, and the spatial gradient in composition can be effectively characterized.
critiques.evidence: Prior work on compositionally graded alloys has shown region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, supporting this approach (e.g., earlier studies on graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys).
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that other co-varying microstructural factors within the graded sample may confound the results, making it challenging to isolate the effect of Mg concentration.
critiques.fix: Implement rigorous local compositional and microstructural mapping (e.g., using TEM/EDS) to decouple Mg effects from other gradient-induced variations.

critiques.addresses_problem: This approach tests whether moderate thermal aging triggers the evolution of a metastable solid solution into a more ordered intermetallic/oxide network, directly linking such evolution to changes in oxidation and corrosion behavior.
critiques.constraints: It adheres to the density and material system constraints by using a MgAlCuZnGd HEA in an as-cast non-equilibrium state with a defined aging step.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is plausible; moderate thermal aging can indeed activate diffusion, leading to the nucleation of Mg-rich precipitates and formation of protective oxide or spinel phases.
critiques.feasibility: Thermal aging and subsequent high-temperature oxidation/corrosion tests are standard procedures in alloy studies and are readily implementable.
critiques.evidence: Previous literature on AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys and similar HEA systems has associated Mg content and phase stability with functional properties, lending support to this methodology.
critiques.main_risk: The primary risk is that the thermal aging parameters (e.g., temperature and duration) might over-drive the transformation, causing full equilibration rather than controlled evolution from a metastable state.
critiques.fix: Introduce a series of aging durations and temperatures to capture the transition window, ensuring that the study remains within the non-equilibrium regime while still triggering the desired transformation.
